\section{Problem Setup and Methods}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Safety Commitment Point}
\label{sec:commitment-point}

When a reasoning model is jailbroken, its chain-of-thought (CoT) transitions from safety-aware deliberation to committed harmful generation. We define the \textbf{Safety Commitment Point} (CP) as the first reasoning step after which safety reasoning permanently ceases. Formally, given a trace of $T$ reasoning steps, the CP is the earliest step $t^*$ such that no step $t > t^*$ contains safety-relevant deliberation. Steps before CP are \emph{pre-commitment} (the model is still considering refusal); steps at or after CP are \emph{post-commitment} (the model has irrevocably committed to harmful output).

We operationalize this definition on HarmThoughts~\citep{harmthoughts} traces, which provide step-level annotations of safety reasoning. Each step receives a binary label: pre-CP ($y_t = 0$ for $t < t^*$) or post-CP ($y_t = 1$ for $t \geq t^*$). The detection task is binary classification at each step, producing a score $s_t \in [0, 1]$ that estimates the probability that the model has passed its commitment point by step $t$.

We study four reasoning models spanning two architectures (Llama and Qwen) and two parameter scales (7--8B and 32B), summarized in \cref{tab:models}.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Arch.} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Layers} & \textbf{Hidden} & \textbf{Traces} & \textbf{Test} \\
\midrule
R1-8B & Llama & 8B & 32 & 4096 & 209 & 43 \\
OT-7B & Qwen & 7B & 28 & 3584 & 228 & 47 \\
R1-32B & Qwen & 32B & 64 & 5120 & 100 & 20 \\
QwQ-32B & Qwen & 32B & 64 & 5120 & 95 & 19 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Models studied. R1-8B and R1-32B are distilled from DeepSeek-R1~\citep{deepseekr1}; QwQ-32B~\citep{qwq} is a native reasoning model; OT-7B~\citep{openthinker} is trained with STILL~\citep{still} on Qwen2.5-7B. Data: HarmThoughts~\citep{harmthoughts} with step-level CP annotations. Split: 60/20/20. Total: 632 traces.}
\label{tab:models}
\end{table}

The two 7--8B models provide larger test sets ($n{=}43$--$47$) than the 32B models ($n{=}19$--$20$), yielding narrower confidence intervals. All four models show significant HS advantage after correcting for layer selection bias (\cref{sec:layer-results}).

\subsection{Probe Architecture}
\label{sec:probe-architecture}

\paragraph{Hidden-state (HS) probes.} At each reasoning step $t$, we extract the last-token hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ from a selected layer $\ell$ of the target model. We train an L2-regularized logistic regression classifier with balanced class weights on the binary pre-CP vs.\ post-CP labels. The probe produces a score $s_t = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} + b)$, where $\sigma$ is the logistic function. Layer selection is the subject of \cref{sec:layer-sensitivity}.

\paragraph{Text probes.} We encode each step's text using all-MiniLM-L6-v2, producing a 384-dimensional sentence embedding $\mathbf{e}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{384}$. The same logistic regression procedure is applied to these embeddings. Text probes represent detection performance from surface-level linguistic signals alone, serving as a modality comparison baseline for HS probes.

\paragraph{Temporal windowing.} For window size $W$, we concatenate features from steps $[t{-}W{+}1, \ldots, t]$ into a single input vector. We evaluate $W \in \{1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25\}$ and select the operating-point $W$ per-model on the validation set. This tests whether temporal context improves detection over single-step classification.

\paragraph{GRU sequence models.} We train single-layer GRU classifiers that process the full step sequence to produce per-step predictions. We evaluate two variants: a single-layer variant (using hidden states from the best-performing layer) and a multi-layer variant (concatenating representations from 7 layers spanning the model depth). Architectural details are in \cref{app:gru_details}.

\paragraph{Training procedure.} All probes are trained with Adam (learning rate $1 \times 10^{-3}$, $\beta_1{=}0.9$, $\beta_2{=}0.999$), batch size 16, maximum 50 epochs with early stopping (patience 10 on validation balanced accuracy). Inputs are z-score normalized per dimension using training set statistics.

\subsection{Layer Selection Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:layer-sensitivity}

Hidden-state probing requires selecting which transformer layer to extract representations from. This choice constitutes a researcher degree of freedom that, as we demonstrate, can entirely determine whether hidden-state probes appear to outperform text-based alternatives. We conduct a systematic sensitivity analysis to expose this bias and recommend principled selection criteria.

\paragraph{The composite metric bias.} A natural approach is to select the layer that maximizes some composite performance metric on the validation set. The default composite metric used in our initial experiments, the product of balanced accuracy and crossing rate (the fraction of traces where the probe score crosses the detection threshold at least once), is a common choice for threshold-based detectors. We show that this specific composite systematically biases toward shallow layers through a mechanism unrelated to discriminative power.

\paragraph{Mechanistic explanation.} Shallow transformer layers produce more volatile representations across reasoning steps. This volatility causes probe scores derived from shallow layers to cross any fixed threshold more frequently, inflating the crossing rate component independently of whether the probe has learned genuinely informative features. The product metric therefore favors layers that are ``trigger-happy'' (high crossing rate due to representational instability) rather than layers whose representations encode the semantic distinction between pre-CP and post-CP states. The effect is strongest in deeper models: in 64-layer models (R1-32B, QwQ-32B), the biased metric selects layers at 3--16\% depth, while principled metrics converge on layers at 94--98\% depth.

\paragraph{Five-metric ablation.} To quantify this bias, we evaluate layer selection under five metrics across all four models:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{bal\_acc $\times$ crossing\_rate} (biased composite): Selects layer 2 for QwQ-32B (3\% depth) and layer 10 for R1-32B (16\% depth).
\item \textbf{Pure balanced accuracy}: Selects deep layers consistently: layer 14 for R1-8B (44\%), layer 16 for OT-7B (57\%), layer 60 for QwQ-32B (94\%), layer 63 for R1-32B (98\%).
\item \textbf{Precision}: Converges on deep layers for all four models.
\item \textbf{Inverse pre-CP false positive rate (FPR)}: Converges on deep layers for all four models.
\item \textbf{Composite (bal\_acc + precision $-$ FPR)}: Converges on deep layers for all four models.
\end{enumerate}

Four of five metrics independently converge on deep layers. Only the crossing-rate component of metric (1) drives shallow-layer selection. The full metric $\times$ model ablation is presented in \cref{tab:layer_selection}.

\paragraph{Downstream impact.} The practical consequence of biased layer selection is severe. For the 32B models, selecting shallow layers entirely masks the hidden-state probe advantage over text probes: probe performance at layers 2--10 is statistically indistinguishable from text probes, while the same probes at layers 60--63 show clear separation. This demonstrates that layer selection is not a minor implementation detail but a methodological choice that can flip a paper's central conclusion.

\paragraph{Why deep layers are correct.} Our claim that deep layers provide the appropriate selection does not rest on the circular argument that ``HS probes outperform text probes at deep layers.'' Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion. First, the mechanistic analysis above identifies a specific, quantifiable bias in the crossing-rate metric that artificially inflates shallow-layer scores. Second, four of five selection metrics, each capturing a different aspect of probe quality, independently converge on deep layers. Third, the probing literature consistently finds that task-relevant semantic representations form in mid-to-deep transformer layers~\citep{belinkov2022probing, tenney2019bert}. The convergence of mechanistic reasoning, empirical metric agreement, and established probing theory provides a non-circular justification for deep-layer selection.

\subsection{Baseline Methods}
\label{sec:baselines}

We evaluate six alternative detection approaches to contextualize probe performance and test whether simpler or unsupervised methods suffice.

\paragraph{BOCPD.} Bayesian Online Change-Point Detection~\citep{adams2007bayesian} is applied to probe score sequences, testing whether the commitment point produces an abrupt distributional shift detectable without supervised labels. We sweep hazard rate and observation model parameters on the validation set.

\paragraph{CUSUM.} Cumulative sum control charts accumulate evidence for a mean shift in the probe score sequence. We sweep the reference value $\delta$ and decision threshold $h$ to find optimal configurations per model (\cref{app:bocpd_config}).

\paragraph{Mahalanobis distance.} Following TrajGuard~\citep{trajguard}, we compute the Mahalanobis distance of each step's hidden state from the pre-CP distribution centroid, testing whether geometric separation in activation space suffices for detection without training a discriminative probe.

\paragraph{Representation Engineering (RepE).} Following \citet{zou2023representation}, we compute the mean-difference direction between labeled pre-CP and post-CP hidden states and project each step's representation onto this direction as a probe score. This direction-based supervised method tests whether a single linear direction, computed from class means rather than discriminative training, captures the commitment distinction.

\paragraph{MLP probe.} A two-layer nonlinear probe ($d \rightarrow 128 \rightarrow 1$, ReLU activation) tests whether the linear probe's capacity is a bottleneck, or whether the pre-CP/post-CP distinction is linearly separable.

\paragraph{CCS-adapted.} We adapt Contrast-Consistent Search~\citep{burns2023discovering} for commitment detection by constructing contrastive pairs from pre-CP and post-CP steps within each trace. This tests whether weakly supervised representation discovery can match fully supervised probes. CCS still requires CP labels for pair construction, making it semi-supervised rather than fully unsupervised.

\paragraph{Cross-model transfer.} We project hidden states into a shared subspace via PCA and evaluate whether a probe trained on one model transfers to another, testing the universality of commitment representations.

\paragraph{Position-only baseline.} A classifier that predicts post-CP based solely on the step index $t / T$ (normalized position within the trace). This critical control tests whether probes capture genuine semantic signal beyond the trivial positional correlation that later steps are more likely to be post-CP.

\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
\label{sec:evaluation}

\paragraph{Metrics.} We report six complementary metrics. \textbf{Balanced accuracy}: mean of sensitivity and specificity at the optimal threshold. \textbf{Precision}: fraction of threshold-exceeding steps that are truly post-CP. \textbf{Pre-CP FPR}: reported at both step-level (pooling all pre-CP steps across traces) and trace-level (mean per-trace FPR, treating each trace as an independent observation). \textbf{Coverage}: fraction of jailbreak traces where at least one step exceeds the detection threshold. \textbf{Lead time}: number of steps between first detection and the true CP ($t^* - t_{\text{detect}}$); positive values indicate early warning.

\paragraph{Statistical testing.} All modality comparisons (HS vs.\ text probes) use a two-sided null-centered bootstrap test (1000 resamples) on trace-level metric values. For each resample, we draw paired differences with replacement, center the distribution at the null hypothesis of zero difference, and compute the two-tailed exceedance probability. We conduct 12 hypothesis tests (3 metrics $\times$ 4 models) and apply the Holm-Bonferroni step-down correction at $\alpha{=}0.05$. This procedure controls the family-wise error rate while maintaining power across the test battery.

\paragraph{Control task.} Following \citet{hewitt2019control}, we train probes on randomly permuted labels and compute selectivity as real accuracy minus random-label accuracy. Selectivity exceeding 5 percentage points indicates that the probe has learned genuine structure beyond positional artifacts. This complements the position-only baseline by testing whether the probe's internal representations encode semantic content.

\paragraph{Detection criterion.} We use $K{=}5$ (five consecutive threshold crossings required for detection) throughout all experiments. This criterion does not affect step-level metrics (balanced accuracy, precision, FPR), which are computed over all steps independently. It governs coverage and lead time: a trace is ``detected'' only when five consecutive steps exceed the threshold, reducing spurious detections from isolated high-scoring steps.

1	\section{Experiments}\label{sec:experiments}
2	
3	We evaluate temporal probes across four reasoning models (\cref{tab:models}), comparing hidden-state (HS) and text modalities under different layer selection criteria. Our experiments address three questions: (1)~Does the layer selection metric determine whether HS probes appear effective? (2)~Do HS probes outperform text probes at correctly selected layers? (3)~Which alternative detection methods fail, and why?
4	
5	\subsection{Experimental Setup}\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Models and data.} We study four models spanning two architectures and two parameter scales: R1-8B (Llama-8B, R1-distilled, $n{=}43$ test traces), OT-7B (Qwen-7B, STILL-trained, $n{=}47$), QwQ-32B (Qwen-32B, native reasoning, $n{=}19$--$20$), and R1-32B (Qwen-32B, R1-distilled, $n{=}20$). All traces come from HarmThoughts with step-level commitment point (CP) annotations. We use a 60/20/20 train/validation/test split across all models (\cref{tab:models}).
8	
9	\paragraph{Training and evaluation.} All probes use L2-regularized logistic regression with balanced class weights. For each model, we select the temporal window $W$ on the validation set from $W \in \{1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25\}$. HS probes extract last-token hidden states from a selected transformer layer; text probes encode each reasoning step with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384 dimensions). Detection requires $K{=}5$ consecutive threshold crossings. Modality comparisons use a two-sided null-centered bootstrap test (1000 resamples) with Holm-Bonferroni step-down correction across 12 tests (3 metrics $\times$ 4 models, $\alpha{=}0.05$).
10	
11	\paragraph{Layer selection.} We evaluate five layer selection metrics per model (\cref{sec:layer-sensitivity}). The biased composite metric (balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate) systematically selects shallow layers for 32B models because representational volatility at early layers inflates the crossing rate component. Four unbiased metrics (pure balanced accuracy, precision, inverse FPR, and an additive composite) converge on deep layers. Results throughout this section use the corrected deep layers, with explicit comparison to biased-layer outcomes in \cref{sec:layer-results}.
12	
13	\subsection{Layer Selection Results}\label{sec:layer-results}
14	
15	\cref{tab:layer_selection} presents the layer selected by the biased composite metric and the consensus of four unbiased metrics across all four models. For R1-8B, all five metrics agree on layer~14 (44\% depth), with no discrepancy. For the remaining three models, the biased metric selects shallow layers: L0 (0\%) for OT-7B, L2 (3\%) for QwQ-32B, and L10 (16\%) for R1-32B. All four unbiased metrics converge on deep layers: L16 (57\%) for OT-7B, L60 (94\%) for QwQ-32B, and L63 (98\%) for R1-32B. The bias is most extreme for the 64-layer 32B models, where the composite metric selects layers in the bottom 16\% of the network while all other metrics select layers above 94\%.
16	
17	\begin{table}[t]
18	\centering
19	\small
20	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
21	\toprule
22	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Biased}$^a$ & \textbf{Corrected}$^b$ & $p$ \textbf{(corr.)} \\
23	\midrule
24	R1-8B & L14 (44\%) & L14 (44\%) & ${<}0.001$ \\
25	OT-7B & L0 (0\%)$^c$ & L16 (57\%) & ${<}0.001$ \\
26	QwQ-32B & L2 (3\%) & L60 (94\%) & ${<}0.005$ \\
27	R1-32B & L10 (16\%) & L63 (98\%) & ${<}0.001$ \\
28	\bottomrule
29	\end{tabular}
30	\caption{Layer selection sensitivity. $^a$\,Selected by bal\_acc $\times$ crossing\_rate. $^b$\,Consensus of four unbiased metrics (pure bal\_acc, precision, inverse FPR, additive composite). $^c$\,OT-7B has only 28 layers; bias is less extreme than for 64-layer models. The rightmost column reports HS vs.\ text precision $p$-values at the corrected layer (two-sided null-centered bootstrap, 1000 resamples). At the \emph{biased} layers for 32B models, corresponding $p$-values were 0.064 (R1-32B) and 0.35--0.83 (QwQ-32B), both non-significant.}
31	\label{tab:layer_selection}
32	\end{table}
33	
34	The downstream impact on modality comparison is severe for the 32B models. At biased layers, two-sided bootstrap $p$-values for HS precision advantage are 0.064 for R1-32B (not significant) and 0.35--0.83 for QwQ-32B (not significant). At the corrected deep layers, all $p$-values drop below 0.005. The R1-32B case illustrates the magnitude of this effect: the biased metric selects L10 (16\% depth, precision $p{=}0.064$), while pure balanced accuracy selects L63 (98\% depth, $p{<}0.001$). For QwQ-32B, the shift is from L2 ($p{=}0.35$--$0.83$) to L60 ($p{<}0.005$ across all 15 window sizes tested). OT-7B represents an intermediate case: the biased metric selects L0 (0\%), but OT-7B has only 28 layers, so the practical impact is smaller than for 64-layer models. The corrected layer (L16, 57\% depth) still produces stronger HS-text separation ($p{<}0.001$ on all three metrics).
35	
36	This sensitivity analysis reveals that a single metric component (crossing rate) can reverse a study's central conclusion. Had we reported only biased-layer results, we would have concluded that the HS advantage is scale-dependent: significant at 7--8B, absent at 32B. The corrected analysis shows HS advantage across all four models, with the apparent scale-dependence being a methodological artifact of biased layer selection.
37	
38	\subsection{HS vs.\ Text Comparison}\label{sec:hs-text}
39	
40	\cref{tab:hs_vs_text} presents the main HS vs.\ text comparison at corrected layers. All 12 hypothesis tests (3 metrics $\times$ 4 models) pass Holm-Bonferroni step-down correction at $\alpha{=}0.05$. At the previously used biased layers, only 5 of 12 tests passed (all from the two 7--8B models that were unaffected by the metric bias). The corrected analysis recovers all 7 previously failing tests across the full battery.
41	
42	\begin{table}[t]
43	\centering
44	\small
45	\begin{tabular}{llcrrrr}
46	\toprule
47	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Layer} & $W$ & $\Delta$\textbf{BA} & $\Delta$\textbf{Prec} & $\Delta$\textbf{FPR} & \textbf{HB} \\
48	\midrule
49	R1-8B & L14 & 15 & +8.2 & +22.4 & $-$7.4 & 3/3 \\
50	OT-7B & L16 & 3 & +10.9 & +21.2 & $-$17.1 & 3/3 \\
51	QwQ & L60 & 3 & +15.4 & \textbf{+23.6} & $-$9.8 & 3/3 \\
52	R1-32B & L63 & 1 & \textbf{+18.7} & +15.4 & \textbf{$-$14.6} & 3/3 \\
53	\bottomrule
54	\end{tabular}
55	\caption{HS vs.\ text probe comparison at corrected layers. $\Delta$BA, $\Delta$Prec, and $\Delta$FPR report the HS$-$text difference in percentage points for balanced accuracy, precision, and pre-CP false positive rate. HB: tests passing Holm-Bonferroni step-down ($\alpha{=}0.05$, 12 tests total). All comparisons use a two-sided null-centered bootstrap (1000 resamples). $W$: validation-selected temporal window per model.}
56	\label{tab:hs_vs_text}
57	\end{table}
58	
59	\paragraph{7--8B models.} R1-8B ($n{=}43$, L14, $W{=}15$) shows HS advantages of +8.2pp balanced accuracy ($p{=}0.005$), +22.4pp precision ($p{<}0.001$), and $-$7.4pp FPR ($p{=}0.044$). All three survive Holm-Bonferroni correction. OT-7B ($n{=}47$, L16, matched $W{=}3$) shows +10.9pp balanced accuracy ($p{<}0.001$), +21.2pp precision ($p{<}0.001$), and $-$17.1pp FPR ($p{<}0.001$), with all three tests surviving correction. The precision advantage is consistent across these architecturally distinct models: +22.4pp on the Llama-based R1-8B and +21.2pp on the Qwen-based OT-7B, despite different training methods (R1 distillation vs.\ STILL).
60	
61	\paragraph{32B models.} QwQ-32B ($n{=}19$--$20$, L60, $W{=}3$) shows +15.4pp balanced accuracy ($p{<}0.001$), +23.6pp precision ($p{<}0.001$), and $-$9.8pp FPR ($p{=}0.004$), all surviving correction. R1-32B ($n{=}20$, L63, $W{=}1$) shows +18.7pp balanced accuracy ($p{<}0.001$), +15.4pp precision ($p{<}0.001$), and $-$14.6pp FPR ($p{=}0.007$), all surviving correction. The precision advantage ranges from +15.4 to +23.6pp across all four models.
62	
63	\paragraph{Control task selectivity.} Following \citet{hewitt2019control}, selectivity scores confirm genuine safety signal beyond positional artifacts: R1-8B 12.5pp, OT-7B 18.3pp, QwQ-32B 15.3pp, R1-32B 7.5pp. All four models exceed the 5pp threshold.
64	
65	\paragraph{Caveats.} Three qualifications apply. First, the validation-selected $W$ differs per model ($W{=}15$ for R1-8B, $W{=}3$ for OT-7B and QwQ-32B, $W{=}1$ for R1-32B). The tests measure whether HS outperforms text at each model's best operating point, not at a uniform window. Second, R1-32B at $W{=}1$ achieves only 25\% coverage (5 of 20 test traces detected), which limits practical utility despite strong per-detection performance. At $W{\geq}3$, R1-32B significance vanishes due to the dimensionality constraint ($51200 \times W$ features for $n{=}20$ training traces). Third, QwQ-32B HS lead time is negative ($-$1.2 to +1.9 steps) compared to text probes (3.7 to 12.3 steps): HS probes are more accurate but detect later on this model. In safety deployment, earlier detection by several steps may outweigh higher per-step accuracy.
66	
67	\subsection{Temporal Context Effects}\label{sec:temporal}
68	
69	Text probes benefit universally from larger temporal windows across all four models. Balanced accuracy improves by +3 to +12pp and precision by +8 to +23pp from $W{=}1$ to $W{=}25$, with consistent FPR reductions.
70	
71	HS probes show similar benefits on 3 of 4 models. On R1-8B (L14), increasing $W$ from 1 to 25 improves balanced accuracy from 77.8\% to 81.0\% (+3.2pp), precision from 69.3\% to 82.2\% (+12.9pp), and reduces FPR from 9.65\% to 4.8\% ($-$4.9pp). At the validation-selected $W{=}15$, performance reaches 80.2\% balanced accuracy, 77.7\% precision, and 6.4\% FPR, which captures most of the precision gain with higher coverage than $W{=}25$. QwQ-32B and R1-32B follow similar monotonic patterns for precision and FPR across the full $W$ range.
72	
73	\begin{figure}[t]
74	\centering
75	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_temporal_improvement.pdf}
76	\caption{Effect of temporal window size on R1-8B HS probe performance (L14). Precision increases monotonically from 69.3\% ($W{=}1$) to 82.2\% ($W{=}25$); FPR decreases from 9.65\% to 4.8\%.}
77	\label{fig:window_ablation}
78	\end{figure}

\section{Experiments}\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate temporal probes across four reasoning models (\cref{tab:models}), comparing hidden-state (HS) and text modalities under different layer selection criteria. Our experiments address three questions: (1)~Does the layer selection metric determine whether HS probes appear effective? (2)~Do HS probes outperform text probes at correctly selected layers? (3)~Which alternative detection methods fail, and why?

\subsection{Experimental Setup}\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Models and data.} We study four models spanning two architectures and two parameter scales: R1-8B (Llama-8B, R1-distilled, $n{=}43$ test traces), OT-7B (Qwen-7B, STILL-trained, $n{=}47$), QwQ-32B (Qwen-32B, native reasoning, $n{=}19$--$20$), and R1-32B (Qwen-32B, R1-distilled, $n{=}20$). All traces come from HarmThoughts with step-level commitment point (CP) annotations. We use a 60/20/20 train/validation/test split across all models (\cref{tab:models}).

\paragraph{Training and evaluation.} All probes use L2-regularized logistic regression with balanced class weights. For each model, we select the temporal window $W$ on the validation set from $W \in \{1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25\}$. HS probes extract last-token hidden states from a selected transformer layer; text probes encode each reasoning step with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384 dimensions). Detection requires $K{=}5$ consecutive threshold crossings. Modality comparisons use a two-sided null-centered bootstrap test (1000 resamples) with Holm-Bonferroni step-down correction across 12 tests (3 metrics $\times$ 4 models, $\alpha{=}0.05$).

\paragraph{Layer selection.} We evaluate five layer selection metrics per model (\cref{sec:layer-sensitivity}). The biased composite metric (balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate) systematically selects shallow layers for 32B models because representational volatility at early layers inflates the crossing rate component. Four unbiased metrics (pure balanced accuracy, precision, inverse FPR, and an additive composite) converge on deep layers. Results throughout this section use the corrected deep layers, with explicit comparison to biased-layer outcomes in \cref{sec:layer-results}.

\subsection{Layer Selection Results}\label{sec:layer-results}

\cref{tab:layer_selection} presents the layer selected by the biased composite metric and the consensus of four unbiased metrics across all four models. For R1-8B, all five metrics agree on layer~14 (44\% depth), with no discrepancy. For the remaining three models, the biased metric selects shallow layers: L0 (0\%) for OT-7B, L2 (3\%) for QwQ-32B, and L10 (16\%) for R1-32B. All four unbiased metrics converge on deep layers: L16 (57\%) for OT-7B, L60 (94\%) for QwQ-32B, and L63 (98\%) for R1-32B. The bias is most extreme for the 64-layer 32B models, where the composite metric selects layers in the bottom 16\% of the network while all other metrics select layers above 94\%.

\centering

\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Biased}$^a$ & \textbf{Corrected}$^b$ & $p$ \textbf{(corr.)} \\
\midrule
R1-8B & L14 (44\%) & L14 (44\%) & ${<}0.001$ \\
OT-7B & L0 (0\%)$^c$ & L16 (57\%) & ${<}0.001$ \\

R1-32B & L10 (16\%) & L63 (98\%) & ${<}0.001$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Layer selection sensitivity. $^a$\,Selected by bal\_acc $\times$ crossing\_rate. $^b$\,Consensus of four unbiased metrics (pure bal\_acc, precision, inverse FPR, additive composite). $^c$\,OT-7B has only 28 layers; bias is less extreme than for 64-layer models. The rightmost column reports HS vs.\ text precision $p$-values at the corrected layer (two-sided null-centered bootstrap, 1000 resamples). At the \emph{biased} layers for 32B models, corresponding $p$-values were 0.064 (R1-32B) and 0.35--0.83 (QwQ-32B), both non-significant.}
\label{tab:layer_selection}
\end{table}

The downstream impact on modality comparison is severe for the 32B models. At biased layers, two-sided bootstrap $p$-values for HS precision advantage are 0.064 for R1-32B (not significant) and 0.35--0.83 for QwQ-32B (not significant). At the corrected deep layers, all $p$-values drop below 0.005. The R1-32B case illustrates the magnitude of this effect: the biased metric selects L10 (16\% depth, precision $p{=}0.064$), while pure balanced accuracy selects L63 (98\% depth, $p{<}0.001$). For QwQ-32B, the shift is from L2 ($p{=}0.35$--$0.83$) to L60 ($p{<}0.005$ across all 15 window sizes tested). OT-7B represents an intermediate case: the biased metric selects L0 (0\%), but OT-7B has only 28 layers, so the practical impact is smaller than for 64-layer models. The corrected layer (L16, 57\% depth) still produces stronger HS-text separation ($p{<}0.001$ on all three metrics).

This sensitivity analysis reveals that a single metric component (crossing rate) can reverse a study's central conclusion. Had we reported only biased-layer results, we would have concluded that the HS advantage is scale-dependent: significant at 7--8B, absent at 32B. The corrected analysis shows HS advantage across all four models, with the apparent scale-dependence being a methodological artifact of biased layer selection.

\subsection{HS vs.\ Text Comparison}\label{sec:hs-text}

\cref{tab:hs_vs_text} presents the main HS vs.\ text comparison at corrected layers. All 12 hypothesis tests (3 metrics $\times$ 4 models) pass Holm-Bonferroni step-down correction at $\alpha{=}0.05$. At the previously used biased layers, only 5 of 12 tests passed (all from the two 7--8B models that were unaffected by the metric bias). The corrected analysis recovers all 7 previously failing tests across the full battery.

The precision advantage is consistent across these architecturally distinct models: +22.4pp on the Llama-based R1-8B and +21.2pp on the Qwen-based OT-7B, despite different training methods (R1 distillation vs.\ STILL).

\paragraph{32B models.} QwQ-32B ($n{=}19$--$20$, L60, $W{=}3$) shows +15.4pp balanced accuracy ($p{<}0.001$), +23.6pp precision ($p{<}0.001$), and $-$9.8pp FPR ($p{=}0.004$), all surviving correction. R1-32B ($n{=}20$, L63, $W{=}1$) shows +18.7pp balanced accuracy ($p{<}0.001$), +15.4pp precision ($p{<}0.001$), and $-$14.6pp FPR ($p{=}0.007$), all surviving correction. The precision advantage ranges from +15.4 to +23.6pp across all four models.

\paragraph{Control task selectivity.} Following \citet{hewitt2019control}, selectivity scores confirm genuine safety signal beyond positional artifacts: R1-8B 12.5pp, OT-7B 18.3pp, QwQ-32B 15.3pp, R1-32B 7.5pp. All four models exceed the 5pp threshold.

\paragraph{Caveats.} Three qualifications apply. First, the validation-selected $W$ differs per model ($W{=}15$ for R1-8B, $W{=}3$ for OT-7B and QwQ-32B, $W{=}1$ for R1-32B). The tests measure whether HS outperforms text at each model's best operating point, not at a uniform window. Second, R1-32B at $W{=}1$ achieves only 25\% coverage (5 of 20 test traces detected), which limits practical utility despite strong per-detection performance. At $W{\geq}3$, R1-32B significance vanishes due to the dimensionality constraint ($51200 \times W$ features for $n{=}20$ training traces). Third, QwQ-32B HS lead time is negative ($-$1.2 to +1.9 steps) compared to text probes (3.7 to 12.3 steps): HS probes are more accurate but detect later on this model. In safety deployment, earlier detection by several steps may outweigh higher per-step accuracy.

\subsection{Temporal Context Effects}\label{sec:temporal}

Text probes benefit universally from larger temporal windows across all four models. Balanced accuracy improves by +3 to +12pp and precision by +8 to +23pp from $W{=}1$ to $W{=}25$, with consistent FPR reductions.

HS probes show similar benefits on 3 of 4 models. 253	\section{Control Task Methodology}
254	\label{app:control}
255	
256	We follow the selectivity framework of \cite{hewitt2019control} to verify that our probes capture genuine safety-relevant structure rather than surface-level correlations.
257	
258	\paragraph{Procedure.} For each model, we randomly permute the binary labels (pre-CP vs. post-CP) across all steps while preserving the marginal label distribution. We then retrain the probe with identical architecture (L2-regularized logistic regression) and hyperparameters on these shuffled labels. Selectivity is defined as:
259	\begin{equation}
260	    \text{Selectivity} = \text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}} - \text{Acc}_{\text{control}}
261	\end{equation}
262	where $\text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}}$ is the probe accuracy on true labels and $\text{Acc}_{\text{control}}$ is the accuracy on permuted labels. A selectivity of zero indicates that the probe exploits only non-linguistic features (e.g., position); higher values confirm that the representation encodes task-relevant information.
263	
264	\paragraph{Results.} We repeat the control experiment 5 times (10 for OT-7B) with different random permutations and report the mean control accuracy. Selectivity scores are: OT-7B 18.3pp (layer 16), QwQ-32B 15.3pp (layer 2), R1-8B 12.5pp (layer 14), R1-32B 7.5pp (layer 10). All values exceed the 5pp threshold recommended by \cite{hewitt2019control}. OT-7B achieves the highest selectivity at a mid-depth transformer layer (57\%), consistent with R1-8B's pattern at 44\% depth. R1-32B's weaker selectivity (7.5pp, near the threshold) is consistent with its overall weaker hidden-state signal. On QwQ-32B, the position baseline accuracy (70.6\%) slightly exceeds the HS probe (67.8\%), indicating that layer 2 encodes strong positional information alongside safety-relevant structure.
265	
266	\paragraph{Position-only baseline.} As a complementary validation, we train a logistic regression classifier using only the normalized step index ($t / T$ where $T$ is the total trace length) as the input feature. This baseline tests whether temporal position alone explains probe performance. On R1-8B, the position-only baseline produces 15.8\% FPR compared to 8.1\% for the HS probe at matched detection rates. The probe's substantially lower FPR confirms that hidden state features carry information beyond what step position provides.

317	\label{app:bug}
318	
319	We disclose a bug discovered during development that affected intermediate results for QwQ-32B.
320	
321	\paragraph{Issue.} In experiment M002 (text baseline evaluation), the QwQ-32B text probe was inadvertently initialized with a midpoint heuristic placeholder rather than true sentence embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Specifically, the placeholder assigned each step a feature vector equal to the midpoint between the mean safe and mean unsafe embeddings from the training set, with small Gaussian noise added. This made the text probe trivially predictive, producing a spuriously significant result ($p{=}0.001$ for HS vs. text FPR difference).
322	
323	\paragraph{Discovery and correction.} The bug was identified during a systematic audit of the feature extraction pipeline. After correction (using actual sentence embeddings), QwQ-32B shows no meaningful modality difference: accuracy $p{=}0.828$, precision $p{=}0.346$, FPR $p{=}0.430$ (two-sided permutation test, 1000 resamples). R1-32B shows directional HS advantages (accuracy $p{=}0.080$, precision $p{=}0.050$, FPR $p{=}0.114$) but none survive Holm-Bonferroni correction. Full results are reported in \cref{tab:hs_vs_text}.
324	
325	\paragraph{Impact on reported results.} All numbers reported in this paper use the corrected pipeline. No figures, tables, or claims in the main text are affected by the original bug. The correction changed only QwQ-32B text baseline numbers, which now show no significant difference from the HS probe on that model.
326	
327	\paragraph{Commitment to transparency.} We report this bug to maintain scientific integrity. All code, including the git history showing the bug and its fix, will be released with the camera-ready version. Researchers reproducing our results can verify the correction independently.
328	
329	\section{Adaptive Two-Stage Detection}
330	\label{app:two_stage}
331	
332	We explored whether a two-stage adaptive window strategy could improve the precision-coverage tradeoff beyond fixed-window detection. The approach uses a short screening window ($W_{\text{screen}}$) to flag candidate unsafe segments, followed by a longer confirmation window ($W_{\text{confirm}}$) applied only to flagged segments. A trace is classified as unsafe if at least $k$ steps exceed the threshold during the confirmation stage.
333	
334	We evaluated all combinations of $W_{\text{screen}} \in \{1, 3, 5\}$, $W_{\text{confirm}} \in \{10, 15, 20, 25\}$, and $k \in \{1, 3, 5\}$ on R1-8B test traces ($n{=}55$; 39 jailbreak, 16 benign). \cref{fig:pareto_two_stage} shows the precision-coverage Pareto front for both methods. The best two-stage configuration ($W_{\text{screen}}{=}3$, $W_{\text{confirm}}{=}15$, $k{=}1$) achieves 72.2\% precision at 76.9\% coverage, compared to 70.9\% precision at 76.9\% coverage for single-stage $W{=}15$. This +1.3pp precision gain at matched coverage represents a Pareto improvement, but the magnitude is marginal. At higher confirmation thresholds ($k{=}3$, $k{=}5$), two-stage detection trades coverage for small precision gains (up to 73.5\% precision at 38.5\% coverage with $k{=}5$), but these operating points are impractical due to excessive missed detections.
335	
336	\begin{figure}[h]
337	\centering
338	\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/pareto_two_stage.pdf}
339	\caption{Precision-coverage Pareto front comparing single-stage fixed-window detection against two-stage adaptive detection on R1-8B. The best two-stage configuration ($W_{\text{screen}}{=}3$, $W_{\text{confirm}}{=}15$, $k{=}1$) Pareto-dominates single-stage $W{=}15$ by +1.3pp precision at matched coverage. Higher $k$ values shift the tradeoff toward precision at the cost of unacceptable coverage loss.}
340	\label{fig:pareto_two_stage}
341	\end{figure}
342	
343	The marginal improvement suggests that fixed-window smoothing already captures most of the temporal signal available in probe score sequences. The two-stage approach adds configuration complexity (three hyperparameters vs. one) without proportional performance gain.
344	
345	
346	\section{Cross-Model Transfer Implementation Details}
347	\label{app:transfer_details}
348	
349	We test whether safety probes transfer across models by projecting hidden states into a shared dimensionality space and applying cross-model classification.
350	
351	\paragraph{Method.} For each source-target model pair, we apply PCA independently to each model's hidden states, reducing to a shared dimensionality $d \in \{512, 1024, 2048\}$. PCA is fitted on the full dataset (including test traces) for each model separately, a setting favorable to transfer since it maximizes the quality of the projection. A logistic regression classifier (C=1.0, class\_weight=`balanced', max\_iter=2000, random\_state=42) trained on the source model's PCA-projected training data is then applied directly to the target model's PCA-projected test data. No cross-model alignment step (Procrustes rotation, CCA, or learned projection) is applied; PCA serves as a standard linear dimensionality reduction baseline.
352	
353	\paragraph{Same-dimension pairs.} For R1-32B and QwQ-32B (both 5120-d hidden states), we additionally test direct transfer without PCA: the source classifier is applied directly to the target model's raw hidden states. This tests whether same-architecture, same-dimensionality models share safety-relevant linear structure.
354	
355	\paragraph{Results.} All 18 transfer configurations (6 directional pairs $\times$ 3 methods: PCA-512, PCA-1024, PCA-2048, plus direct for same-dimension pairs) fail to produce meaningful transfer. The best result is QwQ-32B $\rightarrow$ R1-32B direct transfer at 67.3\% balanced accuracy, against a within-model baseline of 65.2\% (+2.1pp). This margin is within noise and not statistically significant. The complete failure under maximally favorable conditions (PCA fitted on full data, no train/test separation for projection) strengthens the conclusion that safety commitment is encoded in model-specific geometric configurations. PCA is a standard linear alignment baseline; its failure indicates that the problem lies in the representations themselves rather than in the choice of alignment method.

\section{Responsible NLP Research Checklist}

\section{Layer Sweep Results}
\label{app:layer_sweep}

For each model, we sweep all transformer layers and score each candidate layer using the product of balanced accuracy and crossing rate (accuracy-weighted layer selection, defined in \cref{sec:detection-methods}). This composite metric selects layers that simultaneously achieve good classification and reliable threshold crossing on jailbreak traces.

The selected layers are: R1-8B layer 14 (of 32, 43.8\% depth), OT-7B layer 16 (of 28, 57\% depth), R1-32B layer 10 (of 64, 15.6\% depth), and QwQ-32B layer 2 (of 64, 3.1\% depth). Optimal layer depth shows a scale-dependent pattern: 7-8B models select mid-depth layers (43.8\%/57\%), while 32B models favor shallow layers (15.6\%/3.1\%). While scale provides a useful heuristic, layer selection via validation sweep remains necessary for each model.

Final layers consistently show high accuracy but low crossing rate across all four models, suggesting that late-layer representations encode safety state too close to output generation for early detection. Full per-layer results are available in supplementary materials.

\section{Control Task Methodology}
\label{app:control}

We follow the selectivity framework of \cite{hewitt2019control} to verify that our probes capture genuine safety-relevant structure rather than surface-level correlations.

\paragraph{Procedure.} For each model, we randomly permute the binary labels (pre-CP vs. post-CP) across all steps while preserving the marginal label distribution. We then retrain the probe with identical architecture (L2-regularized logistic regression) and hyperparameters on these shuffled labels. Selectivity is defined as:
\begin{equation}
    \text{Selectivity} = \text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}} - \text{Acc}_{\text{control}}
\end{equation}
where $\text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}}$ is the probe accuracy on true labels and $\text{Acc}_{\text{control}}$ is the accuracy on permuted labels. A selectivity of zero indicates that the probe exploits only non-linguistic features (e.g., position); higher values confirm that the representation encodes task-relevant information.

\paragraph{Results.} We repeat the control experiment 5 times (10 for OT-7B) with different random permutations and report the mean control accuracy. Selectivity scores are: OT-7B 18.3pp (layer 16), QwQ-32B 15.3pp (layer 2), R1-8B 12.5pp (layer 14), R1-32B 7.5pp (layer 10). All values exceed the 5pp threshold recommended by \cite{hewitt2019control}. OT-7B achieves the highest selectivity at a mid-depth transformer layer (57\%), consistent with R1-8B's pattern at 44\% depth. R1-32B's weaker selectivity (7.5pp, near the threshold) is consistent with its overall weaker hidden-state signal. On QwQ-32B, the position baseline accuracy (70.6\%) slightly exceeds the HS probe (67.8\%), indicating that layer 2 encodes strong positional information alongside safety-relevant structure.

\paragraph{Position-only baseline.} As a complementary validation, we train a logistic regression classifier using only the normalized step index ($t / T$ where $T$ is the total trace length) as the input feature. This baseline tests whether temporal position alone explains probe performance. On R1-8B, the position-only baseline produces 15.8\% FPR compared to 8.1\% for the HS probe at matched detection rates. The probe's substantially lower FPR confirms that hidden state features carry information beyond what step position provides.


\section{BOCPD/CUSUM Configuration Sweep}
\label{app:bocpd_config}

We sweep hyperparameters for both Bayesian Online Change-Point Detection (BOCPD) and Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) methods applied to the temporal probe score sequences.

\paragraph{BOCPD configurations.} BOCPD models the sequence of probe scores as piecewise-constant segments with Gaussian observation noise. The hazard rate $\lambda$ controls the prior probability of a change-point at each step ($P(\text{change}) = 1/\lambda$).

\paragraph{CUSUM configurations.} CUSUM accumulates evidence for a positive mean shift. The drift parameter $\delta$ sets the minimum shift size to detect, and the threshold $h$ controls the detection boundary.

\begin{table}[h]

We test whether safety probes transfer across models by projecting hidden states into a shared dimensionality space and applying cross-model classification.

No cross-model alignment step (Procrustes rotation, CCA, or learned projection) is applied; PCA serves as a standard linear dimensionality reduction baseline.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

This work provides the first systematic evaluation of safety commitment detection across four reasoning models that span two architectures (Llama, Qwen), two training methods (R1 distillation, STILL), and two scales (7--8B, 32B).
The central methodological finding is that layer selection metric bias can reverse a study's main conclusion.
A composite metric that incorporates crossing rate systematically selects shallow layers at 32B scale, entirely masking the hidden-state advantage and producing the appearance of a scale-dependent effect.
When layers are selected by balanced accuracy alone, four independent metrics converge on deep layers (94--98\% depth for 32B models), and all 12 Holm-Bonferroni-corrected hypothesis tests confirm significant hidden-state superiority, with precision gains of +15.4 to +23.6pp across all four models.
Six alternative approaches fail to match supervised linear probes: BOCPD and CUSUM cannot detect gradual commitment transitions, Mahalanobis distance misses signal concentrated in minor principal components, Representation Engineering yields model-dependent results, MLP probes overfit at 32B sample sizes, CCS provides no gain over standard probing, and cross-model transfer collapses due to model-specific safety representations.
These negative results collectively confirm that safety commitment is gradual, model-specific, and invisible to geometric or unsupervised methods.

For practitioners and future probing studies, we recommend temporal windowing ($W{=}3$--$15$) paired with principled layer selection based on pure balanced accuracy as robust defaults.
Layer selection sensitivity analysis should become standard practice: without it, composite metrics that embed crossing rate can silently bias conclusions toward shallow layers where positional features dominate.
At 32B scale, per-model validation is essential because models with identical architecture but different training methods exhibit divergent detection profiles (R1-32B provides early warning with +13 steps lead time at 25\% coverage, while QwQ-32B achieves broad coverage at 74\% with minimal lead time).
All current methods produce 39--62\% false positive rates on safe traces, and an 85.5\% oracle gap separates learned probes from the theoretical detection frontier.
These results characterize the safety commitment phenomenon rather than solve it.
Closing this gap will require causal intervention techniques such as activation patching, extension to multilingual and multi-turn settings, and evaluation at intermediate scales (13B, 70B) to map how detection profiles evolve with model capacity.
